species.name: Humpback whale
species.range: New York Bight and, at times, harbor waters. Gotham Whale documents returning individuals; a profile is not a current sighting.
species.traits: Baleen plates strain small prey from water. Long flippers and distinct tail markings help researchers recognize individuals.
species.action: Observe at a distance and report marine wildlife to Gotham Whale.

species.name: Harbor seal
species.range: Coastal New York and New Jersey; a regional winter and spring visitor.
species.traits: A rounded head and spotted coat help distinguish this true seal. Resting on shore is normal behavior.
species.action: Watch from a distance; keep pets away and never feed or approach a resting seal.

species.name: Gray seal
species.range: North Atlantic coasts, including regional New York waters in the colder months.
species.traits: A longer muzzle helps distinguish gray seals from harbor seals. Both use shorelines to rest.
species.action: Give hauled-out seals room to rest and let trained responders assess animals in distress.

species.name: Atlantic sturgeon
species.status: ESA Endangered · New York Bight population
species.range: The Hudson River belongs to the New York Bight distinct population segment. These fish move between rivers and coastal waters.
species.traits: Rows of bony plates armor the body. Adults return to rivers to spawn; the mouth is on the underside.
species.action: Support clean-water projects and report unusual or stranded fish to the responsible wildlife agency.

species.name: Shortnose sturgeon
species.range: The Hudson is one of the rivers supporting this protected species.
species.traits: A bottom-feeding fish with bony plates and a short snout. Most of its life is spent in rivers and estuaries.
species.action: Learn the identification differences and leave protected fish undisturbed.

species.name: American eel
species.range: Fresh, brackish, and coastal waters connect its life cycle to the Atlantic.
species.traits: A long-bodied fish whose migration links inland waters and the ocean. The image is a USFWS scientific illustration.
species.action: Support stream connectivity and local water-quality stewardship.

species.name: Hudson River water nymph
species.range: Freshwater tidal habitat in the Hudson River system. No Jersey City occurrence is claimed here.
species.traits: Also called Najas muenscheri. This submerged aquatic plant has fine branching stems and narrow leaves.
threats: Loss of suitable freshwater tidal habitat
species.action: Protect aquatic habitats; leave plants in place and avoid spreading aquatic invasive species.

species.name: Eastern oyster
species.range: New York Harbor is a focus of oyster-reef restoration.
species.traits: Oysters filter suspended material and their reefs provide structure for other organisms. Restoration oysters are not for eating.
species.action: Explore Billion Oyster Project’s organized volunteering and school programs.

places.name: Liberty State Park
places.description: The Richard J. Sullivan Natural Area protects 36 acres, mainly salt marsh. Look for tidal changes, marsh plants, and wildlife using the water’s edge. Check the Nature Center’s programs for guided observation.
places.transit: Take Hudson–Bergen Light Rail to Liberty State Park station. The ferry area is approximately a one-mile walk away; other park destinations have different distances.
places.access: Use the NJDEP visitor guide to choose an accessible entrance and facilities. The regular 2026 shuttle season ended September 6; check the schedule before relying on a shuttle.

places.name: Hudson River Waterfront Walkway
places.description: Follow the public waterfront to watch tides and the meeting of city and estuary. Look from the path and keep wildlife observations at waterfront level.
places.transit: Exchange Place is a starting point served by PATH and Hudson–Bergen Light Rail. Choose your destination and check the trip planner before leaving.
places.access: Conditions vary by section. Consult the Conservancy’s current maps and access information; do not assume a continuous, step-free route through construction areas.

places.name: Lincoln Park & Hackensack wetlands
places.description: Lincoln Park West includes restored native salt marsh beside the Hackensack River. Look for the contrast between tidal wetland, open water, and park habitat. Use established public paths and observation areas.
places.transit: Use NJ TRANSIT’s planner with Lincoln Park, Jersey City as the destination. The western wetland is a separate walk from many bus stops; plan the park crossing.
places.access: Check Hudson County’s park information for current paths and facilities. A fully step-free route to every wetland viewpoint has not been verified for this guide.

places.name: Reservoir 3
places.description: The city reopened the historic reservoir in September 2024. Fresh water, shoreline plants, and surrounding vegetation create a different habitat from the saltwater harbor. Observe from the public perimeter path.
places.transit: Use NJ TRANSIT’s planner with Reservoir 3, Jersey City as the destination, then confirm the entrance and the walking connection.
places.access: The city reports an ADA-compliant widened perimeter path and a new connecting bridge. Check current opening and access information before a class trip.

challenges.title: Water: when the pipes fill
challenges.problem: Combined sewers carry rainwater and sewage through the same pipes. Heavy rain can exceed their capacity, sending mixed overflow into waterways. This is a design and capacity problem in shared infrastructure.
challenges.response: EPA’s January 2022 agreement announced sewer repairs, more capacity, and climate-resilient design. It also included replacement of over 12,000 lead drinking-water pipes, a separate system being improved alongside the sewers. These are commitments, not a completed-work count.
challenges.action: Support rain gardens and tree stewardship that help manage runoff. Keep litter out of drains and join organized cleanups.

challenges.title: Trees & summer heat
challenges.problem: Paved surfaces absorb heat, while tree shade and vegetation help cool the city. Uneven tree cover means that people do not all experience the same summer conditions.
challenges.response: Jersey City’s urban-forest program and urban forestry grant support planting, care, and canopy restoration. Older canopy estimates use different dates and methods; this guide does not present them as a current citywide measurement.
challenges.action: Join supervised tree care through Sustainable Jersey City and follow the city’s guidance for street trees.

challenges.title: Flooding: making room for water
challenges.problem: Coastal storms, high tides, heavy rain, and limited drainage can combine to cause flooding. A mapped flood zone is one part of that picture; flooding can occur outside it.
challenges.response: Jersey City participates in regional resilience planning. The Liberty State Park restoration also aims to strengthen flood resilience through restored habitat and landscape design.
challenges.action: Learn the city’s flood planning resources with your class and take part in public discussions about parks and drainage.

challenges.title: Industrial history & soil
challenges.problem: Historic fill and industrial uses left contamination in parts of Liberty State Park. NJDEP’s chromium program documents site-specific cleanup history in Hudson County. These records describe soil and past land uses, not the people who live nearby.
challenges.response: NJDEP’s park program pairs remediation with habitat restoration. Work includes managing contaminated soil and clean cover as part of preparing the interior for future public use. Construction areas remain separate from visitor routes.
challenges.action: Stay on open public paths and follow NJDEP project updates. Join stewardship activities in areas approved for public use.
